theme: Doctrinal Pause: Justification by Faith Alone
summary: The forensic declaration of righteousness; imputation of Christ’s righteousness; faith alone in Christ alone by grace alone
readingInstruction: Read Romans 3:21-31, Romans 4:1-8, and Galatians 2:15-21. Today is a doctrinal pause on justification by faith alone. Notice the legal language, the word “counted,” and what Paul says about works and grace.
settingTheScene: Justification by faith alone was the central issue of the Protestant Reformation. Martin Luther called it “the article by which the church stands or falls.” It is also the point at which Paul argued against those who wanted Gentile believers to take on the Jewish law. In Galatians, Paul confronts Peter in Antioch because withdrawing from Gentile believers implied that faith in Christ was not enough. The three passages together show that being right with God has always been by grace through faith.
observation: “But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law” (Romans 3:21).
“And are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 3:24).
“So that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).
“For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law” (Romans 3:28).
“For what does the Scripture say? Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness” (Romans 4:3).
“And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness” (Romans 4:5).
“A person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ” (Galatians 2:16).
“If righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose” (Galatians 2:21).
doctrinalFocus:
To justify is to declare righteous. It is a courtroom word, not a hospital word. It describes a change of status, not of nature. In justification, God declares the sinner to be in the right, forgiven and accepted, on the basis of Christ’s work and not our own. The Reformers described this as imputation: our sin is counted as Christ’s, and his righteousness is counted as ours. Paul uses the word “counted” (or “reckoned”) eleven times in Romans 4. The great exchange happens at the cross. God does not pretend we are righteous. He treats us as righteous because Christ is righteous in our place.

Faith is the instrument, not the cause. We are justified by grace (the source), through Christ’s blood and obedience (the ground), and through faith (the means). Faith does not earn anything. It is the empty hand that receives. And “alone” means that nothing is added to faith as a condition for being right with God. But the faith that justifies is never alone; it produces works. James 2 makes this point: a claim to faith that produces no obedience is dead. Paul and James are not opposed. Paul speaks of how we are declared righteous; James speaks of how true faith is shown to be real.

Justification is once for all. The verdict of the last day is announced in advance to those who believe. “Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God” (Romans 5:1). Not “will have” but “have.” Christians have long differed here with Roman Catholic teaching, which holds that justification includes a lifelong process of being made righteous through grace-enabled works and sacraments. Evangelicals hold that sanctification follows justification and does not form part of it. Scholars today also debate the “new perspective” on Paul, which emphasizes the inclusion of Gentiles; most evangelicals receive its insight about covenant community while insisting that Paul is also teaching how sinners stand right before a holy God.
interpretation:
Paul says that righteousness from God has been manifested “apart from the law.” This does not mean the Old Testament was wrong. It means the Law and the Prophets “bear witness to it.” They pointed forward to this. The righteousness comes through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe, without distinction.

Then Paul turns to Abraham, the father of the Jewish people, to prove that justification by faith is not a New Testament novelty. “What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God.” He quotes Genesis 15:6: “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.” Wages are earned and owed. A gift is received. “To the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness.” Notice how startling the phrase “justifies the ungodly” is. Under Old Testament law, a judge who acquits the guilty is condemned (Proverbs 17:15). Yet God does exactly this, because the penalty has been paid.

Paul then brings David as a second witness. In Psalm 32, David speaks of the blessing of the one “whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin.” Forgiveness of sins and counted righteousness are two sides of the same coin.

In Galatians 2, Paul states the truth in personal terms. “We know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law.” And he draws the conclusion: “I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose.” To add anything to faith as a requirement is to say that the cross was not enough. Those who try to be justified by the law are, in effect, setting aside Christ’s death.

This doctrine is the believer’s comfort and the church’s boast. It does not make light of sin. It takes sin so seriously that it required the death of God’s Son. And it gives certainty: our standing before God does not rise and fall with our performance, but rests on Christ.
connection: Genesis 15:6 is the verse behind Romans 4 and Galatians 3. Habakkuk 2:4 stands behind both letters. Psalm 32:1-2 is David’s blessing of the forgiven. Isaiah 53:11 says the righteous one will make many to be accounted righteous. Jeremiah 23:6 calls the coming king “The LORD is our righteousness.” 2 Corinthians 5:21 describes the exchange. Philippians 3:8-9 speaks of having a righteousness not my own. Ephesians 2:8-9 and Titus 3:4-7 teach salvation by grace through faith. James 2:14-26 describes faith that works.
application:
Write in your own words the difference between being declared righteous and being made righteous. Say it to someone this week.

When you feel guilty after failing, remind yourself that your standing before God rests on Christ’s work, not on your record.

Thank God for “counted as righteousness.”
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he justifies the ungodly.
Tell him you bring nothing but faith, and even that is his gift.
Ask him to keep you from trusting in your works.
